title: Shared form in simple organisms need not imply common descent

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Shared form in simple organisms need not imply common descent

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The assumption that similar or identical forms indicate genealogical relationship is far less well founded for minute organisms with few, simple characters whose form is largely produced directly by a physical force, so identical forms of such organisms in different times or places need not indicate unbroken descent or common stock.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: when we attempt to extend it to minute organisms whose specific characters are few and simple, whose simplicity becomes much more manifest when we regard it from the point of view of physical and mathematical description and analysis, and whose form is referable, or (to say the least of it) is very largely referable, to the direct and immediate action of a particular physical force.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Species, form and genealogy”. Scope: minute organisms such as foraminifera (e.g. Lagena), infusoria and radiolaria

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-19: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is measurable, but 'physical force' and 'simple characters' require interpretation. Public phylogenetic and fossil records cover useful subsets, while a clean test of common descent is confounded by taxonomy, preservation, and incomplete linkage of form to genotype.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify morphological complexity and similarity in minute organisms, then test whether genetically distant or independently sampled lineages converge on identical simple forms more often than complex forms do.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Preservation and taxonomic practice can create apparent form identity.

Morphological descriptions and molecular samples rarely come from the same individuals.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Molecular trees and large image libraries can show whether identical simple tests recur in distant lineages, which is the genealogical content of the claim. The further assertion that a physical force produced those forms is not a variable in these archives, and ciliates are far more thinly covered than planktonic foraminifera. A full refutation across minute organisms and geological time would need a compilation the present databases only partly support.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place foraminifera, radiolaria and ciliates in a morphospace and on phylogenies built from molecular sequences. Repeated origin of the same simple forms in lineages that those sequences separate would support the claim; form-twins that are consistently monophyletic once characters are few would weigh against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Taxonomic practice still splits some of these groups by the same simple outlines the claim says are physically forced.

Soft-bodied infusoria lack a fossil record, so the deep-time half of the claim is testable mainly for mineralized skeletons.
